title: State Department Establishes Task Force to End Birth Tourism
summary_raw:
Office of the Spokesperson
Fact Sheet


			
			


			
			
August 12, 2026
Under President Trump and Secretary Rubio’s leadership, the Department of State is using all available tools to defend the integrity of U.S. citizenship, ensure nonimmigrant visas are used only for their lawful and intended purposes, and prevent their exploitation through birth tourism. As President Trump has made clear, citizenship is not a commodity to be acquired through the calculated exploitation of U.S. immigration laws. The Department of State is working closely with the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to combat birth tourism and protect the integrity of the U.S. immigration system. 
New Birth Tourism Prevention Task Force 
To maximize the success of this comprehensive effort, the State Department has established a Birth Tourism Prevention Task Force.
The Birth Tourism Prevention Task Force reviews the activities of visa holders worldwide to identify instances of birth tourism, take action to revoke visas of those who engage in or facilitate it, and dismantle the networks that profit from this abuse.
The Task Force addresses the abuse by analyzing and connecting information held across the Department and other federal agencies, including the DHS.
Thanks to the coordination of the Task Force, the Department of State is addressing birth tourism on a global scale, examining travel histories of individuals from all around the world in order to end this exploitation and abuse.
The Birth Tourism taskforce has taken action by revoking more than 600 visas from foreign nationals across the globe to safeguard our nation from this abuse.
The Department generally revokes visas when there are indications of a potential ineligibility.
The Secretary has broad discretionary authority to revoke visas – and the Trump Administration is committed to exercising that authority to protect the American people and the integrity of our immigration system.
Birth Tourism Has Become a For-Profit Industry 
Facilitators have turned birth tourism into a lucrative, for-profit industry.
These facilitators sometimes market themselves as doulas, midwives, or wellness advocates while openly advertising “birth in the U.S.” services, visa coaching, and hospital arrangements.
Some forge medical documents or coach clients to conceal their true travel purpose and avoid paying hospital bills, with online marketing promising clients “automatic citizenship” and “a future without borders.”
The facts are clear – birth tourism is a pervasive practice that involves nationals from countries spanning every region of the globe.
The Department is taking action to dismantle these networks and hold all participants accountable.
Birth Tourism Fraud 
The work of the Bureau of Consular Affairs Task Force and consular officers at U.S. embassies and consulates around the world is exposing widespread patterns of deception.
Foreigners who willfully misrepresent the purpose of their travel or entry into the United States may be permanently ineligible for a U.S. visa or entry to the United States.
The Department has uncovered patterns that illustrate the lengths some applicants will go to circumvent our laws in order to secure U.S. citizenship for their children – and potentially for themselves in the future.
One couple used a conference and a vacation trip to go shopping as cover stories to give birth to two children in the United States, lying about their travel purpose in two separate visa applications. On the second occasion, the couple concealed that they had a child.  The visas have been revoked.
In another case, a foreign government official requested a visa to travel on behalf of her government for just one week, but instead stayed three months and gave birth in the United States before departing. The Department revoked the visa.
Another traveler applied for a visa to go on vacation in Orlando and instead traveled to Los Angeles and gave birth five days after arrival. The Department revoked the visa.
Citizenship is not a commodity to be acquired through calculated exploitation and evasion of the immigration laws.  Foreign nationals who abuse the visa system, and those who help them do so, may lose their visa, their access, and their future in the United States. This is only the beginning.

title: Pax Silica AI Assistance Project NOFO
summary_raw:
Office of the Spokesperson
Media Note


			
			


			
			
August 12, 2026

At the Second Pax Silica Summit in Washington, D.C. on June 25-26, Under Secretary of State for Economic Affairs Jacob Helberg announced a new Pax Silica AI Assistance Project to more efficiently and rapidly move high-value AI inputs through Panama.  The Department has published a competitive Notice of Funding Opportunity for this ambitious new platform that has the potential to transform how trusted partners transship rapidly critical goods that power the AI economy of the 21st century.  Working with Congress, the Department seeks to commit up to $50 million in foreign assistance funding to strengthen global AI supply chain security by developing an AI supply chain credentialing and provenance platform that expedites the shipping of semiconductors, AI infrastructure, critical minerals, and related products in participating Pax partner countries and economies. We are putting our resources behind our vision and demonstrating that trusted partnership is backed by real investment.
The Pax Silica AI Assistance Project would begin as a pilot, implementing an AI supply chain credentialing platform with Panama’s ports and customs authorities. If the pilot with Panama is successful, a second phase of the project would expand the geographic reach of these platforms to other Pax Silica countries and economies.
Interested bidders are encouraged to apply for this Notice of Funding Opportunity (NOFO) at Opportunity Listing – Pax Silica Artificial Intelligence Assistance Project before the NOFO closes on August 20.  This deadline is firm and will not be extended.  Any questions from potential bidders regarding the NOFO should be directed to PaxFund-NOFO-DL@state.gov.

title: Joint Statement by Secretary of Health and Human Services Robert F. Kennedy and Secretary of State Marco Rubio: United States to Serve as Secretariat of the Geneva Consensus Declaration
summary_raw:
Marco Rubio, Secretary of State
Robert F. Kennedy
Press Statement


			
			


			
			
August 12, 2026

As the Secretariat of the Geneva Consensus Declaration returns to the United States, we express our deep appreciation to Hungary for its exceptional stewardship. Hungary has faithfully safeguarded the Declaration and its principles, and we are grateful for its leadership and commitment to expanding the Declaration’s signatories.
The United States will carry this work forward through a whole-of-government effort led jointly by the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services and the U.S. Department of State. The Secretariat will be housed within the Office of Global Affairs at the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services.
Established in 2020, the Geneva Consensus Declaration, led by the United States, began as a joint initiative with a few like-minded countries. Today the group has grown to include more than 40 signatories.
The Declaration has four main objectives: to secure meaningful health and development gains for women; to protect life at all stages; to defend the family as the fundamental unit of society; and to work together across the UN system to realize these values.
The Trump Administration is committed to supporting families, promoting women’s health, and protecting children at all stages of life. Investing in women’s health and well-being saves lives, allows women and girls more opportunities, and protects the family as the fundamental unit of society.

summary_raw:
Marco Rubio, Secretary of State
Washington, D.C.
Thomas Jefferson Room
Interview


			
			


			
			
August 11, 2026

QUESTION:  Hi, everyone, and welcome to this week’s episode of The Katie Miller Podcast.  We’re at the State Department today, joined by Secretary of State Marco Rubio and his beautiful wife Jeanette.
SECRETARY RUBIO:  It’s good to be with you, finally.
QUESTION:  I know.  So excited.  So you briefly just said you’d have a career in podcasting after this.
SECRETARY RUBIO:  I don’t know yet.  I mean, I’m going to see how this one goes and then we’ll play it from there.  But it won’t be about politics.  It might not even be about foreign policy.
MRS RUBIO:  Sports.
SECRETARY RUBIO:  Sports, yeah.  College football, cultural things.
QUESTION:  You’ve joked about your career after politics.  What do you think it would be?
SECRETARY RUBIO:  I don’t know, obviously.  I hadn’t even thought about that yet.  But I love the sports stuff, so I’d be – I’d love to be involved in, like, the intersection of sports and culture.  But basica lly, whatever pays the most.
QUESTION:  Anything to do the Fox News?
SECRETARY RUBIO:  (Laughter.)  I’d like to do the commercials on Fox.  That’s one of our inside jokes is I’m always – I always look at the commercials that are running on Fox, whatever they’re advertising, like a rain gutter or whatever, and I’m like, I think I could be the pitch – if I could line two or three of those, two or three of those alone, I’m probably set for a while.  So I think I could be the pitchman, like, whatever William Devane is selling.  (Laughter.)  He’s got his big thing going.  So I have my eye on that.  We’ll see.
QUESTION:  Jeanette doesn’t do many interviews, so thank you for doing this.  What did you think about his move from being a senator to Secretary of State?  Were you on board the second he brought it up or did you take some convincing?
MRS RUBIO:  No, I was on board.  I was because of everything that’s going on in our country.  And so I was totally on board when he told me that this is something he was considering.
QUESTION:  What’s easier, being a Senate spouse or being the wife of the Secretary of State?
MRS RUBIO:  I think they’re both different.  I would say being a Senate spouse is probably easier just because there were less events; there were things that I didn’t have to do, being now in D.C.  But they’re both – they were both – they’re both great.
SECRETARY RUBIO:  You asked the wrong question.  You have to ask which one was more fun.
QUESTION:  Which one was more fun?  (Laughter.)
MRS RUBIO:  Being – now.  Being a Secretary of State spouse.
QUESTION:  You get a lot of praise for how you hold yourself and the events that you’ve gone to with Marco.  Most recently there was a viral moment where you handed him your phone in India.  (Laughter.)
MRS RUBIO:  I did.  I did.
QUESTION:  What other things does he carry for you besides your phone?
MRS RUBIO:  Oh, my gosh, a lot of things.
SECRETARY RUBIO:  I’ve had makeup.
MRS RUBIO:  Yes, my makeup.  Yeah, because those purses are so small, so you can’t fit a lot of things in there.
SECRETARY RUBIO:  But it looks weird.  Like, if the outline comes out, you have, like, this – people think I walk around with, like, mascara and compact on my pockets.
MRS RUBIO:  Which is why I —
SECRETARY RUBIO:  It’s like, this guy is really vain.  (Laughter.)
MRS RUBIO:  So I learned that I do it in public so he can’t say no.  (Laughter.)
SECRETARY RUBIO:  Yeah.  But I’ve been fully loaded.  There’ve been times where I have a phone and then I have, like, the compact thing here and then the other makeup here and then the little crayon thing —
MRS RUBIO:  No, that’s not true.
SECRETARY RUBIO:  Not crayons, but the liner or whatever.
MRS RUBIO:  Not true.  Usually it’s one or two things.
QUESTION:  Does he carry a ring light every so often?  Is he a good photographer?
MRS RUBIO:  Oh, no.  No, no, no.  No.
SECRETARY RUBIO:  What do you mean, like cell phone photography?
MRS RUBIO:  Like —
QUESTION:  Yeah.  Are you good at cell phone photography?
SECRETARY RUBIO:  Oh, she has one of those light things too.  Remember?  I had one of those in my pocket one time.
MRS RUBIO:  I did, but I don’t ever really use it.
SECRETARY RUBIO:  And I thought it was like a foreign listening device.  (Laughter.)  Like, oh, my God, they bugged me, what is this thing in my pocket?  And then I realized that was, like, a light you attach to your phone.  But for about 10 seconds I thought I had been, like – a tracking device had been dropped in my pocket by somebody, so —
QUESTION:  What’s on your playlist right now?
SECRETARY RUBIO:  That’s a really good question.  I haven’t been able to update my playlist, but I love – I say this like – people think whatever.  I love a lot of electronic music because it fuses classical, increasingly it does country music.  So I like a lot of the remixes of, like, songs that you’ve heard over the – there’s this EDM mix of Ring of Fire which is really good.  So I like that stuff.
So I listen to a little bit of everything except for, like – I don’t hate it, okay?  I’m not against it. I’m not anti-country music, but that’s not my thing.  She loves it.  She loves country.
MRS RUBIO:  I love country music.  I do.
SECRETARY RUBIO:  I think it’s just very sad.  Most of the songs are about, like, somebody whose wife and dog left them and so —
MRS RUBIO:  Well, that’s not true.  You need to listen to more Morgan Wallen and others because that’s not true.
SECRETARY RUBIO:  Well, some of the time, certainly.  Some of them are good.
QUESTION:  So who picks the radio in the car, you or Jeanette?
SECRETARY RUBIO:  Well, I don’t have a radio in the car.  She listens to radio, but I don’t have a radio in the car ride. 
MRS RUBIO:  Yeah.
SECRETARY RUBIO:  I can’t have a – I mean, because it’s – you’re always talking or you’re on the phone.  But generally she’ll decide, irrespective of who’s driving, which violates one of the great rules of the universe, right?  Like, the driver gets to – but not if you’re with her.  She gets to decide what you’re going to listen to, and it’s —
MRS RUBIO:  That’s not true.  You – you get – you put your music on as well.  (Laughter.)
SECRETARY RUBIO:  She says my music gives her a headache, so —
QUESTION:  Who’s your favorite rapper?
SECRETARY RUBIO:  Of all time?
QUESTION:  Yeah.
SECRETARY RUBIO:  I mean, just from an artistic standpoint – and obviously, he never lived long enough to know what he would’ve turned into, but Tupac was very, very talented, I thought.  And he was actually very talented, not just – people forget.  I mean, he was, like, trained to be an actor as well.  I think he went to, like, that school in New York or in Baltimore.  I forgot exactly where he went to high school, but he went to a artistic high school, and you can see that later on when he played a number of roles in a number of movies over the years, including the one with Janet Jackson, that he was a good actor.  He was a good lyricist in terms of the lyrics that he wrote.  He left a lot of music, some of which has still not been released, that his family holds.  So I thought he was a very talented person, primarily because I think he was a narrator more than anything else of a certain point of view and lifestyle, or upbringing and worldview.  So I think of all time he’s probably my favorite.  There’s a lot of other very talented people.
QUESTION:  Have you ever thought about your own rap name?
SECRETARY RUBIO:  Me?
QUESTION:  Yeah.
SECRETARY RUBIO:  No, I don’t think —
QUESTION:  Have you ever considered Lil’ Marco?
SECRETARY RUBIO:  What?
QUESTION:  Have you ever considered Lil’ Marco?
            PRESIDENT TRUMP:  Little Marco, Little Marco.
SECRETARY RUBIO:  No, I haven’t.  I haven’t thought about it.  I mean, I wouldn’t be a good rapper, but I probably could be a good producer in terms of, like, identifying talent and so forth.  But I don’t know, maybe not.
But – but yeah, some of the modern – like, the younger people that are out there now I’m really not as familiar with because the whole hip-hop genre has changed quite a bit.  And it’s not for the worse or the better, I’m just saying it’s changed.  But the ’90s were great.  The only problem with the ’90s is they all – they’re like – these people, like, were shooting at each other, like, for real.  Like, it wasn’t just in their lyrics, especially when the whole Death Row thing and the East Coast thing developed over time.  So I grew up in that era, and it’s a little different than it is now, even though some of these guys still get in trouble.  But anyway —
QUESTION:  What’s life like as Secretary of State and National Security Advisor?
SECRETARY RUBIO:  Every day is different, right?
MRS RUBIO:  Yeah.
QUESTION:  So you wake up in the morning, and what happens when you’re both here in D.C.?
SECRETARY RUBIO:  Well, it depends what time you wake up in the morning because the way the world is, like, sometimes you’ll – “wake up in the morning” means 2:30 because there’s something going on at, like – it’s prime time somewhere else.  So sometimes that’s what wakes you up.  It also depends, although we’ve been pretty busy on the national security front because of Iran and before that other things, but there’s no single typical day.  Typically weekends are just a little slower, obviously but – and then the President has an insane work schedule.  Like, he works every day, all day.  You guys know that, too.  So he doesn’t really have, like, days off or vacation time.  There is really no slow time when it comes to national – international affairs.
So no day is typical, but generally speaking, if I had to plan a day, I would start – I start here at the State Department in the mornings and then try to be over at the White House before or shortly after noon and when the President really gets humming.  And then obviously – or sometimes in the mornings he does a lot of foreign leader calls, so I’m on a lot of those calls in the morning.  Those are sometimes as early as 7:00 a.m.  So —
QUESTION:  When you wake up at 2:30 in the morning, do you wake Jeanette up as well?  And then what do you do during that time?  Do you go back to sleep?
SECRETARY RUBIO:  No, she might hear the phone ring.  Or she might hear it —
MRS RUBIO:  Yeah, I hear the phone ring but I don’t wake up.  No.
SECRETARY RUBIO:  She doesn’t – no.  All that —
MRS RUBIO:  He gets up when he needs. 
SECRETARY RUBIO:  Yeah, I’ll go to another room.  I’m not going to – but – and that doesn’t happen every day.  I don’t want to exaggerate, but it happens.  And then sometimes the phone call is just to tell you can you go down to your classified phone or whatever so you can get the news from there.  So then you know it’s, like, for real.  So anyway.
QUESTION:  I don’t think most people realize that when you were a senator, Jeanette stayed back in Florida.  What was that decision like, and how is that working now with his schedule?
MRS RUBIO:  So the decision was made because we figured we wanted to keep our kids with the same day-to-day routine and their environment and not change anything.  So that was the compromise that we made. 
I think the kids are older now.  They’re all graduated from high school and now they’re in school, in universities.  So now it’s different.  I mean, now it’s easier for me because I’m able to now be a part of more of what he’s doing, and I think it was the best decision.  It was the best decision for our kids.  I  mean, he would come down also when he was a senator, down on weekends, and I think he liked it as well because it kept him grounded around his constituents, wouldn’t you say?  And also see his family.
QUESTION:  What was he like as a dad of  different stages?
MRS RUBIO:  Oh, my gosh.
QUESTION:  So what was your favorite —
MRS RUBIO:  He’s a prankster.  He would prank my kids.
QUESTION:  What’s the best prank?
MRS RUBIO:  Oh, my gosh.  He would do —
SECRETARY RUBIO:  But they would prank me.  I mean, they’re pretty good at it too, so.
MRS RUBIO:  He would scare them.  He would just hide.  He would just go to any room and they would walk down the hallway and then all of a sudden he would pop out, and he was always doing things like that.
SECRETARY RUBIO:  The thing is if you scare your kids – I mean, okay, this is going to —
MRS RUBIO:  This is just weird.  (Laughter.)  This is weird.  This is – this is not normal.
SECRETARY RUBIO:  Okay.  But listen – listen to – if you scare your kids when they’re young repeatedly in the right settings – I’m not talking about, like, mortal death, mortal threat, but then over time they become desensitized to —
MRS RUBIO:  Or need counseling.  (Laughter.)
SECRETARY RUBIO:  No, no, no, no.  None of  my kids – they’ve become desensitized.  So, like, nothing surprises them.  And so —
MRS RUBIO:  Okay.  Yeah, well, yes, they’re – they’re ready.
SECRETARY RUBIO:  Yeah.
MRS RUBIO:  According to Marco Rubio’s theory.  But – but no, I mean, we had a lot of fun and we have four kids.  They all had different personalities, and when Marco would come down it would cause a great stir.
QUESTION:  It’s been the summer of babies in the West Wing.  What was Marco like when you guys were first having kids?  Do you have any good stories for having babies?
MRS RUBIO:  He was good.  He was good.  When he – he would help me especially as they multiplied, right?  So when – so I would get my sleep and he would put on the alarm, and he would – when he was doing his speeches he would wake up, he would get the baby, right, and he would feed the baby at night sometimes for me.  I mean, the majority of the time I did it, but he would help me a lot.  He did.  That he was very good at.
QUESTION:  What was your favorite age of parenting?
SECRETARY RUBIO:  Look, there are times – like, you know when you’re on your phone, like, you’ll get those memory pictures that pop up?  And I always tell people, like, I would give a lot of money for one more day, like just 24 hours of that era.  And so that was fun when they were little because you remember that part of them.  But I also enjoyed, especially with the boys in some respects, the sort of the adolescent high school years because they were involved in sports and I had a chance to be a part of some of that.  So that was fun.
But I think every stage, every season of life has its own – like, I always tell people one day you’ll look back at this and say these are the good old days, and that’s true of every stage. 
MRS RUBIO:  It’s true.
SECRETARY RUBIO:  You look back at every time, and when you’re in the middle of it you don’t realize it.  And then —
MRS RUBIO:  And it goes by so fast.  It really does.
SECRETARY RUBIO:  Ten years from now, we’re going to be looking back at these times and say, oh, remember we were in Washington and the kids this, that, and the other.  So I think you almost – probably one of the things that I learned over time is you try to appreciate the moment that you’re in right now, because that moment’s not going to come back.  And every stage and every – every season of life has its things that you should enjoy.
So I don’t know if I had a favorite.  They were all very different.  And it was easier when they were little because they kind of didn’t have schedules and you’d just scoop them up and take them where you’re going.
MRS RUBIO:  Yes.
SECRETARY RUBIO:  As they got older, they had activities and things they had to do.
MRS RUBIO:  And they wanted to do your – they wanted to do everything you were doing.
QUESTION:  Were the kids ever embarrassed of him?
SECRETARY RUBIO:  Embarrassed?
MRS RUBIO:  I don’t think so.  I don’t – no.
QUESTION:  Because he tells a lot of jokes, right?  Like, what’s your best dad joke?
MRS RUBIO:  No, but they have —
SECRETARY RUBIO:  I don’t have – I don’t do dad jokes.  My jokes are either good or – I mean, I don’t —
MRS RUBIO:  No, he doesn’t – he likes – no.  He is a dad that would come home and, like, whatever the kids were going to do, he was going to do.  Like, he loves scary movies, he loves those – and my kids, of course, I would say no to them, and he would say let’s do it.  So that’s —
SECRETARY RUBIO:  Again, desensitization.
MRS RUBIO:  Exactly.  (Laughter.)
QUESTION:  So who’s the strict parent?
SECRETARY RUBIO:  She is.
MRS RUBIO:  I am.
QUESTION:  What does he give in easily on when the kids were younger? (Laughter.)
MRS RUBIO:  Everything.  (Laughter.)
SECRETARY RUBIO:  Not everything, but —
MRS RUBIO:  No, I mean, obviously when – there’s boundaries, right?  But I mean, for the most part he’s the one let’s them get away or do whatever they want.
QUESTION:  So what’s the family group chat like these days?  Is it a bunch of, like, memes going back and forth?
SECRETARY RUBIO:  It is actually our kids generally making fun of each other.
MRS RUBIO:  Oh, yeah.
SECRETARY RUBIO:  They’re very —
MRS RUBIO:  My kids banter a lot.  Yeah, they – so everybody’s opining in something that’s going on.
SECRETARY RUBIO:  But my – the two middle ones.  So my oldest one and my youngest one are not the greatest at bantering.  I mean, they – it’s not natural, like they don’t naturally enjoy doing it.  But my second one, Daniella, my daughter, and then my third, Anthony.
MRS RUBIO:  Oh, my gosh.
SECRETARY RUBIO:  Especially them two, but also just generally, to the point where it’s uncomfortable sometimes, the stuff they say about each other, to each other.  So —
MRS RUBIO:  It’s fine.
SECRETARY RUBIO:  And which reminds me I’ve got to go back and delete all the stuff because I can’t say —
MRS RUBIO:  No, it’s not that bad.  But it’s fine.  It’s fine.  I mean, this is – every stage has its great moments.  And then, of course, as they get older you get sad, but at the same time you’re proud of them.
QUESTION:  What’s your favorite Marco meme?
MRS RUBIO:  Oh, my gosh, I have – there’s so many of them.  I don’t know.  Obviously, the ones when he’s sitting on the chair, or the ones with the President and the Vice President.  Those make me laugh as well.
SECRETARY RUBIO:  No, but you mean of the ones of me sitting in the chair.
MRS RUBIO:  I mean, the one —
QUESTION:  No, I get that. 
MRS RUBIO:  There’s so many of them.
QUESTION:  There’s so many.
MRS RUBIO:  Right, yes.
QUESTION:  But which is your favorite?  Of all the ones of him sitting on the couch —
SECRETARY RUBIO:  I don’t keep track of them.  Honestly, I don’t do a lot of social media, like, myself, but so I don’t just track that stuff, but people send them to me all the time.
MRS RUBIO:  Or even the baby ones, that – they make me laugh as well.
SECRETARY RUBIO:  Oh, those – yeah, that baby thing, whatever.
QUESTION:  Did you see the WNBA one this morning?
SECRETARY RUBIO:  Somebody might have sent me that one.  At this point it’s like – I think they’re running out of material.  (Laughter.)  But the truth is that – there – I don’t remember if there was, like, a favorite one.  But some are very creative.
MRS RUBIO:  There’s a lot of them.  It’s impressive what they can do.
SECRETARY RUBIO:  I know.  Well, it’s not – I don’t know about – because it’s not you in the picture. 
MRS RUBIO:  I feel like it’s impressive – (laughter).
SECRETARY RUBIO:  So anyway.
QUESTION:  What’s the most surprising thing about being Secretary that nobody warned you about?
SECRETARY RUBIO:  The interesting thing is – again, it’s the – it’s a different job, but when you’re in the Senate for 14 years doing foreign relations, you know a little bit about how the place happens and works.  I think that the breadth and scope of the State Department, and power in particular, it wasn’t surprising.  It was revealing to me because you sort of perceived it, but you didn’t realize, like, there’s a lot that other agencies do that requires the State Department to either okay or sign off on or initiate.  And so I think that’s surprising to me. 
The other – I wouldn’t say it’s surprising, but I came to appreciate it more, is a lot of the customer service work we do, because people think of the State Department as, like, diplomacy, and it is.  But we also do passports.  We also help people all over the world in the consulates and embassies – American travelers somewhere and they get in trouble or have a bad situation, and we help them. 
So I think you come to appreciate, like, the professionalism of the people that do that work and how valuable it is, because for a lot of Americans their only interaction ever with the State Department will be the day they lose their passport, or the day they realize they have a cruise on Saturday morning and it’s Friday and they haven’t – they didn’t renew their – they didn’t renew their passport.  So I think I’ve come to appreciate more that part of the job that the State Department does.

QUESTION:  How long did it take for you to figure out the State Department?
SECRETARY RUBIO:  Figure out the State Department?
QUESTION:  Yeah.  Like, navigate it, figure it all out, unpack it all.
SECRETARY RUBIO:  Well, I think that’s still a learning process.  I mean, along the way we’ve also done a – what I think was a very important reorganization of it, to bring it back more to its core principles.  I think we did a lot of things that previous secretaries of state – many of whom will never admit it – wish they could have done in terms of, like, bringing foreign aid together with foreign policy so that they’re both pushing in the same direction.
QUESTION:  Did any of your predecessors give you advice coming into the job?
SECRETARY RUBIO:  A few.  I mean, I don’t know “advice” is the right term; I think they gave me their impressions.  But I think so much of what we do here is dependent on the times in which you live.  If you were secretary of state in the middle of the Cold War, or secretary of state post-9/11, that’s a very different world from what we’re facing right now.  So I think there’s some things they can give you advice on in terms of, like, how they managed their schedule and how – but ultimately the secretary of state works for the president.  And so a lot of what you do in this job, and what this place does, should be geared and aligned and built around what the president – who the president is.  And so a – a Department of State under President Trump is – should look different than it looks under the next president, what it’s going to look like under the next president, or previous presidents.  It should be a reflection of the foreign policy direction that the current president wants to take it.

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Oh, me, big-time. 
MRS RUBIO:  (Laughter.)  Oh, please.  That’s not true. 
SECRETARY RUBIO:  Are you kidding me?  But I’ll say almost anything to move past it, whatever it was.  Like, I – she has great memory and stuff, and I don’t.  So for example, like –
MRS RUBIO:  (Laughter.)  That is not true.
SECRETARY RUBIO:  — she can recall something that happened in 1999; on September of ’99, do you remember when you said or did this?  And I’m like, no, I – actually I don’t remember this.  And so she has an incredible sort of catalogue of – (laughter) – grievances that she’s able to use at appropriate times.  As I, on the other hand, I – my preference is generally to move on from things quickly.  Like, you deal with it off – you get mad, you get whatever, and then you just move quickly on it. 
So – but I don’t know.  I mean, look, you asked that question about marriage.  Marriage is not a – unfortunately people watch a lot of movies and stuff, and they think that marriage is about, oh, just two people that are always happy and always – I mean, it’s life.  You make —
MRS RUBIO:  Right.
SECRETARY RUBIO:  You entered into a partnership to share life, and life is hard.  There’s ups, there’s downs, there’s good days, there’s bad days, there’s great moments, there’s difficult moments, there’s disagreement.  All of that is – so it takes, for lack of a better term, maybe it’s cliche-ish, but it really is a commitment to say, okay —
MRS RUBIO:  It’s a commitment. 
SECRETARY RUBIO:  — we’ve agreed to live life and share life together, not just because you care about one another, but because of the commitment we’ve made to one another.  And then you have to sort of ride that through.  And there – a lot of times, unfortunately, I think people have been given this idealistic view that there – it’ll always be – every day will be phenomenal.  And that’s just not true.

MRS RUBIO:  (Laughter.)  No, I didn’t buy them.  He bought them.  He – I never bought them.  You bought them for me.

MRS RUBIO:  It’s been a problem.  It’s a problem in our home, exactly.  It’s — 
SECRETARY RUBIO:  I need to be asleep by a certain time so that I can wake up by a certain time.  I don’t need 12 hours of sleep, but I need sleep.

MRS RUBIO:  No, I don’t.  I just don’t think about it.  I just keep going.  Yeah.  He’s —

MRS RUBIO:  Oh, my gosh.

QUESTION:  So what’s the secret to raising happy, well-adjusted, conservative children?
MRS RUBIO:  You have to talk to them.  You have to debate with them.  You have to let them tell you what their thoughts are.  And usually we would do that when we would sit down and eat, right?  I mean, that’s when our conversations would take place.  And they would all —
SECRETARY RUBIO:  My kids talk a lot.
MRS RUBIO:  Yes, and give us their thoughts.
SECRETARY RUBIO:  And they like to talk at the same time.  So literally, like somebody’s – it happens all the time, and it’s a source of some frustration. 
MRS RUBIO:  It’s true, it’s true. 
QUESTION:  But one child will be speaking, and literally, like, 10 seconds in, a second one will jump on and then start talking at the same time, potentially about a different topic. 
MRS RUBIO:  It’s true. 
SECRETARY RUBIO:  And then a third one will jump in.  And so the whole place sounds like – it’s just nuts.  And at some point, I’ll have to stop and say hold on, someone was just speaking.  There’s not a lot – I don’t know if that even answers your question.  These are – we’re just airing grievances now.  (Laughter.)  But – no, but I think the – this is an interesting question.  There are a lot of downsides to being in public service, which I have been basically the entirety of my kids’ lives.  That’s the – the time, right?  You can’t be in two places at once.  So you will miss things.  And I think this is true of many careers. 
But I think the benefit of it, at least, is the kids know that we’ve been doing meaningful things.  Like we haven’t been – I haven’t been gone because I’m on a hunting trip every weekend with my friends and not hanging around.  They know that what I do is meaningful.  And I think as they’ve gotten older, they’ve – whether they – they’ve appreciated that part of it.  And so whatever it is they choose to do in their life, I think, will be built on the idea that the purpose of life is to do meaningful things with the time you have and the opportunities that you have. 
And sometimes meaningful things mean you’ll make money, but sometimes it means you’re not making as much money as someone else but you’re doing things that are really important.  And so I hope that that – and the thing people forget about parenting is that the most important thing a parent does is not what you say.  It’s what they see you do. 
MRS RUBIO:  A hundred percent. 
SECRETARY RUBIO:  Like for me, the most important lesson I learned from my father – he wasn’t the kind of guy that would sit you down and give you a long talk or whatever.  I just saw my dad got up every morning and went to work somewhere.  And two weeks out of the year, he didn’t have to work because he got a vacation, but every other day and week of the year, it involved him getting up on time and showing up somewhere and working, even on the days he didn’t want to go, I’m sure.  That alone is one of the most important life lessons you’ll learn, and it’s stunning to me how many people don’t learn that.
MRS RUBIO:  But to add to your question, it really is challenging them, because they do have their thoughts and their views, and allowing them to have them and then respond to them.  And that’s what we would do, and it’s worked.  My kids are great when it comes to the way – their beliefs, and we’re all pretty aligned, honestly.

QUESTION:  Who’s your best friend in the administration?

QUESTION:  Yeah, that you can tell. 
SECRETARY RUBIO:  I don’t know if it’s funny.  I mean, look, I think there’s been some times on Air Force One – like, I remember coming back from China.  I’m not going to say who the person was, but this person was sleeping on one of the couches in the conference room.  And for a significant period of this flight, it was debatable whether this person had passed away or not, depending on how they’re sleeping.  (Laughter.)  I mean, I – I couldn’t see chest movement.  I couldn’t see, like, that there – I couldn’t establish a consistent breathing pattern in the individual, but I also didn’t want to wake them up on the one hand or discover a dead body on the other. 
So we spent a considerable – like 90 minutes sort of debating, should we make a move?  Should I call the doc?  Should we deal with this?  Because it’s embarrassing if you wake him up – oh, I was just sleeping.  But if they were dead, like, what do you do?  You have a dead body on the plane.  Who’s going to – what do you deal with that?  I don’t know what the protocol is for it.  Luckily, the person was fine and there was no such – so I don’t know if it was funny, but there was a lot of debate about how to approach this particular topic, because there was a lot of noise going on, the lights were on, and this person was not responding to any of the stimulus.  And the breathing pattern was difficult.  You could see every now and then that there was, like, maybe a breath, but I just – like, I don’t know you sustain life at that pace of respiration.  So I don’t know if it was funny, but — 
MRS RUBIO:  Were you watching him the whole time? 
SECRETARY RUBIO:  I kept tabs on it.
QUESTION:  I kept tabs.
SECRETARY RUBIO:  Because I just figured, like, I need to account for where I was when this person passed away.
MRS RUBIO:  Oh, my gosh. 
SECRETARY RUBIO:  Because there’s going to be an investigation and I don’t want – but luckily it all worked out. 
QUESTION:  Of all the cabinet members we’ve interviewed, every single one said you’re the funniest person in the administration.  Literally every single one.  What’s your best joke, or a joke that you’ve told? 
SECRETARY RUBIO:  So here’s the thing.  A lot of the jokes that people consider funny, they’re inside jokes.  They wouldn’t make sense for people in their everyday life because they’re things that have happened internally that people view or – and so they – but I don’t know if these are jokes or not jokes, but like, I – I don’t know.  I can say this to you.  Like, I’m a big Bobby Kennedy fan.  I think he’s one of the best people I’ve ever met.  Like, the guy truly is pure of heart.  So I always – every now and then I’ll tell Bobby, “Bobby, before I met you —
MRS RUBIO:  He’s great.
SECRETARY RUBIO:  — I thought you were crazy because that’s what people would say about you.”  I said, “Now I believe half your stuff.”  (Laughter.)  So he thinks that’s really funny.  I don’t think that’s, like, a big joke or anything, but I tell him that.  And I think Bobby’s one of the most fantastic people I’ve ever met, just such a good, good guy who really is well-intentioned in everything he does and really smart. 
QUESTION:  The Vice President says you have a big sweet tooth.
MRS RUBIO:  Oh, my gosh. 
QUESTION:  I assume you haven’t adopted RFK’s diet of red meat and fermented vegetables? 
SECRETARY RUBIO:  No.  No, this is a crazy diet.  This is a – this is a diet that consists of eating sauerkraut and meat.  Now, you understand, like, this is not a sustainable thing.  Like, you can’t just walk into a —
MRS RUBIO:  Well, he sustains it because he does it. 
SECRETARY RUBIO:  Can you imagine – he – but he has to travel with coolers of sauerkraut. 
MRS RUBIO:  But he does.  He does.
SECRETARY RUBIO:   I’m not going to travel the world with a cooler full of sauerkraut.  It’s ridiculous.  I can’t do it.  It’s not sustainable for — 
QUESTION:  Are you MAHA? 
SECRETARY RUBIO:  I’m in favor of MAHA.  Like, I think people should be healthy. 
MRS RUBIO:  No, he is not. 
SECRETARY RUBIO:  But I think ultimately, at the end —
MRS RUBIO:  He is completely not.  I —
QUESTION:  What’s he eat?
MRS RUBIO:  Pop-Tarts.  
SECRETARY RUBIO:  No, I don’t eat Pop-Tarts every day. 
MRS RUBIO:  Okay, you eat sweets.  You —
SECRETARY RUBIO:  The Pop-Tart is one of the great American innovations in the history of the world, if you think about it.  It comes in this beautiful foil package. 
MRS RUBIO:  He eats all the things you should not be eating, every single thing. 
SECRETARY RUBIO:  Like what?  Like, what do I eat that I should not be eating? 
MRS RUBIO:  Okay. 
SECRETARY RUBIO:  Like other than ice cream. 
MRS RUBIO:  Anything.  Anything that – anything that’s sugar, you will take it down.
SECRETARY RUBIO:  You need carbohydrates to function.  (Laughter.)  And I would —
MRS RUBIO:  He will. 
SECRETARY RUBIO:  I did – I — 
MRS RUBIO:  He loves fast food.  He loves it all. 
SECRETARY RUBIO:  Okay.  I did – at one time maybe four or five years ago, I tried this thing called keto.  You’ve heard of this?  Okay. 
QUESTION:  Yeah, keto. 
SECRETARY RUBIO:  And you just eat all this protein, and so you go through this massive withdrawal from sugar and carbohydrates for the first 72 hours.  It was a near-psychotic event for me. 
MRS RUBIO:  (Laughter.)  It’s true.  It’s true.  
SECRETARY RUBIO:  Like, if I did this in this job, I would be, “Mr. President, we must bomb Paraguay.”
MRS RUBIO:  It’s true. 
SECRETARY RUBIO:  And it’s like, “Why?”  “I don’t know, I’m just really mad; I haven’t had any sugar.”  (Laughter.)  So the point is that you can’t – it really is not as – I’m not against this diet.  I’m not asking that we ban it.  I encourage people to try it.  I’m just saying it’s not for everyone.  That’s what I’m saying.  (Laughter.)
QUESTION:  I asked the Vice President and Dr. Oz this, so I’m curious:  Is the hot dog a sandwich? 
SECRETARY RUBIO:  Is the hot dog a sandwich? 
QUESTION:  Yeah, 57 percent of Americans believe that a hot dog is indeed a sandwich. 
SECRETARY RUBIO:  Well, it is a – it’s meat constrained by two pieces of bread, on both sides.
MRS RUBIO:  Yeah, I would say technically it is.  Yeah. 
SECRETARY RUBIO:  So —
QUESTION:  That’s what Merriam-Webster says, by the way, too. 
SECRETARY RUBIO:  That it is a – that it is a sandwich? 
MRS RUBIO:  Yeah. 
SECRETARY RUBIO:  It is. 
QUESTION:  How do you pick your clothes out in the morning? 
SECRETARY RUBIO:  Well, I’m colorblind, so I can’t tell, like, certain colors, like green and blue or black and blue or – so I have trouble doing that.  So generally speaking, the suits are all dark for the most part.  So it’s – I have them ordered. 
QUESTION:  How do you tell which Florsheims go with which outfit? 
SECRETARY RUBIO:  Oh, there’s only – I mean, there’s the one – there’s two Florsheims that we got.  One is the tuxedo, and that’s – that I can tell.  It’s very shiny.  I’m not going to wear that.  And then the other one, so it’s the other one. 
QUESTION:  It’s the last question we ask everyone on the pod. 
SECRETARY RUBIO:  Okay.
QUESTION:  If you could host a dinner party with three people, dead or alive, who’s sitting at the table and what are you eating? 
SECRETARY RUBIO:  A dinner party? 
QUESTION:  Mm-hmm. 
SECRETARY RUBIO:  Well, look, as a Christian I would say Jesus, obviously, but that would be a very unique dinner, and I would probably just want to do it one on one.  (Laughter.)  I don’t want to have a dinner with Jesus and, like, two other people.  It’s like, it’d ruin – the whole vibe gets ruined.  I want that one on one.  So let’s put that one aside for a moment.  (Laughter.)
I would say I’d be – I’d be fascinated at a – there are various combinations that I could put together.  From a political combination, I would say Thatcher, Reagan, and Churchill in the same – it would be really fascinating to hear American president —
QUESTION:  Interesting you don’t put Jeanette. 
SECRETARY RUBIO:  No, no, you said three people that —
MRS RUBIO:  Yeah, it is interesting.
SECRETARY RUBIO:  No, no, but I figure these are people I don’t —
MRS RUBIO:  I’m alive.  She said dead or alive. 
QUESTION:  I said dead or alive. 
SECRETARY RUBIO:  I understand, but that —
MRS RUBIO:  Yeah, but I am alive. 
SECRETARY RUBIO:  But the context of the question was a dinner that you couldn’t already do.  
QUESTION:  No, I know.  I’m giving —
SECRETARY RUBIO:  Like, this would be a very unique situation.  Okay. 
QUESTION:  I’m giving you a hard time.  (Laughter.) 
SECRETARY RUBIO:  And then in the realm of, like, athletics, I would love to do a dinner – because I’m a big fan of, like, athletic excellence, because it’s not just a physical ability, it’s the time they put into it.  I think Kobe Bryant would have been a fascinating person to talk to; Nick Saban, another high driver in that field and the field of athletics; and then probably the third person that I think would be very fascinating to have in there because of his competitive nature is Magic Johnson. 
So those three in a room and just pick their brain about what it took and for – to reach the pinnacle of their careers in athletics.  Because I think there’s analogies to anything you choose in life, right?  In order to be great at something, you have to give up something.  You can’t have both.  There’s things you can’t do in order to do things you want to do.  So it would be fascinating to talk, and two of them are alive; obviously Kobe is not. 
QUESTION:  And what are you eating?  
SECRETARY RUBIO:  Probably sauerkraut and steak.  (Laughter.)  No, I’m joking.  I don’t know.  I mean, but something that’s easy to eat so that —
QUESTION:  What’s the best thing Jeanette makes? 
SECRETARY RUBIO:  Jeanette makes breakfast, fantastic breakfasts.  She’s very good at breakfast.  That’s her specialty, big time.  That said, I mean, I go for the Pop-Tart because it’s much quicker, it’s much more efficient.  (Laughter.)  But —
MRS RUBIO:  Exactly. 
SECRETARY RUBIO:  I don’t eat Pop-Tarts every day.  This is an exaggeration.  If they’re available – like, right now we have no Pop-Tarts at the house, so I’m not eating Pop-Tarts.  
MRS RUBIO:  Because I haven’t bought them.  I haven’t purchased them.
SECRETARY RUBIO:  I don’t go out of my way to buy them, but if they are available, they are very reliable.  Because you’re talking about a 30-second process – bang, bang – and then it comes out, it’s ready.  So, but she makes excellent breakfast, particularly like scrambled eggs, but she does it in a very unique way. 
MRS RUBIO:  What about dinner? 
SECRETARY RUBIO:  Yeah, but you do that far less – dinner.  She’s done it well.  I mean, you do.  Like, you made —
MRS RUBIO:  I know.  Because you go out — 
SECRETARY RUBIO:  I’m not a big fish-eating person, but she made salmon the other day.  It was really good. 
MRS RUBIO:  Yeah, he doesn’t like fish.  
SECRETARY RUBIO:  I don’t like – I mean, it’s not – I’m not anti – like, I’m not against fish.  It’s just not my thing.  But I’ll eat it. 
QUESTION:  Next headline:  “Marco Rubio Is Anti-Fish.” 
SECRETARY RUBIO:  No, no, no, I – fish is good for you, apparently. 
MRS RUBIO:  He is into meat.  That’s his thing. 
QUESTION:  Who’s at your dinner party? 
MRS RUBIO:  Who’s at my dinner party?  Oh, my gosh. 
SECRETARY RUBIO:  Three people, alive or dead, at your dinner party. 
MRS RUBIO:  Oh, my gosh, I don’t know.  I would say people that I loved – my grandmother. 
SECRETARY RUBIO:  Oh, this blew up my answer.  (Laughter.)  This is terrible.  I should have thought of that too. 
MRS RUBIO:  I would say my – my grandmother; of course Christ; and my dad. 
QUESTION:  And what are you making or what are you eating? 
MRS RUBIO:  What am I eating?
QUESTION:  Yeah. 
MRS RUBIO:  Salmon.  (Laughter.) 
QUESTION:  Thank you so much for doing this. 
SECRETARY RUBIO:  Thank you, it was fun. 
QUESTION:  Thanks for watching this episode of the Katie Miller Podcast.  Don’t forget, we’re every Tuesday night at 6:00 p.m.  See you then.

title: United States Mobilizes Life-Saving Response to Colombia Earthquake
summary_raw:
Office of the Spokesperson
Media Note


			
			


			
			
August 11, 2026

The Trump Administration has mobilized an immediate response following the devastating 7.4 magnitude earthquake that struck regions of Colombia on August 10. Within hours of the earthquake, the Department of State announced $15.5 million in life-saving emergency shelter, food, and protection assistance, in addition to post-earthquake structural assessments. The Department also activated a Disaster Assistance Response Team (DART), which includes humanitarian experts from across the State Department. Members of the DART began arriving in Colombia the day of this devastating earthquake, underscoring the Department’s commitment to immediate, life-saving action in the critical hours following natural disasters in our hemisphere. The State Department continues to liaise with Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella and the Colombian government as it assesses the impacts of and responds to this earthquake.
Disaster Assistance Response Team Deployment
The Department is deploying a DART to provide world-class disaster response expertise, technical and programmatic support, operational leadership, and on-the-ground coordination. The DART is responsible for assessing conditions, identifying humanitarian needs, and leading the U.S. Government’s disaster response. The DART is working closely with existing Department assistance personnel, as well as diplomats at our Embassy in Bogota to coordinate with local authorities and partner organizations.
Life-Saving Humanitarian Assistance Through Trusted Partners
In response to the earthquake, the State Department is mobilizing an initial $15.5 million in life-saving emergency shelter, food, and protection assistance, in addition to post-earthquake structural assessments through trusted partners, including Catholic Relief Services (CRS), the International Organization for Migration, Miyamoto International, the UN World Food Program, and World Vision. Of the $15.5 million in life-saving assistance, $3 million provided through CRS draws from the previously announced CRS global assistance award. With funding already on hand through its global award, CRS can respond immediately through support from the State Department. Additionally, as part of the Department’s $3.8 billion contribution to the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA), the United States provided $200 million to the Colombia Pooled Fund, which OCHA can use to address earthquake-related needs as well as preexisting humanitarian needs in Colombia.
Supporting Americans in Colombia
The Trump Administration has no higher priority than the safety and security of Americans. The Department of State is working tirelessly to provide consular assistance to U.S. citizens and their families in the affected areas. Americans in Colombia should enroll in the Smart Traveler Enrollment Program (STEP) at STEP.state.gov to receive safety and security updates from the U.S. Embassy. They should follow @TravelGov and @USEmbassyBogota on social media for the latest information. The U.S. State Department’s Bureau of Consular Affairs maintains a call center for Americans seeking information or assistance in connection with the Colombia earthquake: call from within the United States 888-407-4747, or from all other locations +1 202-501-4444.
